goal_text: Write a PRD for my side project

nodes.title: Frame the problem
nodes.one_liner: What problem this solves, for whom, and why now

nodes.title: Define what success looks like
nodes.one_liner: How you'll know it worked—goals and signals

nodes.title: Draw the scope line
nodes.one_liner: What's in v1, what's explicitly out

nodes.title: Spell out the core requirements
nodes.one_liner: What it must do—features as user-facing capabilities

nodes.title: Surface assumptions and open questions
nodes.one_liner: What you're betting on and still unsure about

nodes.title: Decide what to build first
nodes.one_liner: Sequencing, milestones, and the minimum slice

nodes.title: Record key decisions and tradeoffs
nodes.one_liner: Choices made and rejected alternatives, for future-you

outline.rationale: The user is experienced with scoping projects but wants a structural understanding of PRD sections used as a personal thinking tool. I skip "what is a PRD / what is a PM" framing and team-alignment/stakeholder-pitch sections per the confirmed understanding. The seven nodes map to the canonical PRD skeleton reframed as decision-forcing sections: problem framing, success definition, scope boundaries, requirements, assumptions/risks, prioritization/sequencing, and a decision log. These are MECE—problem (why), success (measure), scope (boundaries), requirements (what), assumptions (uncertainty), sequencing (order), decisions (rationale) have low content overlap. I ordered them by natural dependency: you can't scope before framing the problem, can't prioritize before listing requirements. The "decision log" node leans into the solo-audience angle—a PRD for future-you benefits from recorded reasoning. I deliberately dropped enterprise-heavy sections (approvals, GTM, detailed specs/wireframes) and project-type-specific content since a generic transferable structure was confirmed as the aim.
